newsitem.title: USA: Interview - Gramlich sees challenges for Fed.
newsitem.headline: Interview - Gramlich sees challenges for Fed.

text.p: Federal Reserve board nominee Edward Gramlich said Thursday that the central bank's biggest challenges include determining how long the economy can sustain low unemployment with low inflation and how the growth of electronic monetary transactions will affect output.
Gramlich, 58, a professor of economics and public policy at the University of Michigan, was one of two people nominated to the powerful Fed boad by President Clinton.
In a brief telephone interview with Reuters, Gramlich said the Fed must determine whether the current "welcome news" of low unemployment with low inflation can be sustained indefinitely.

"We've been able to get our unemployment (down) without having renewed inflation, and whether that's just good luck, whether its temorary or whether its permanent, that's one huge issue facing the Fed," Gramlich said from his office in Ann Arbor, Mich.
He declined to reveal his views on the answer to that question or discuss potential future Fed policy actions.
He also said the Fed must determine the effects of electronic transactions on the traditional relationship between the money supply and economic output.
"Another important issue is that the relationship between changes in money and changes in output is potentially very different in an age when a lot of transactions are conducted electronically."
He said the effects of changes in the money supply could be substantially different as more transactions are done electonically.

"Suppose people don't use money such any more to conduct transactions. It may have a very different role now," he said. "It used to be kind of a leading indicator as to what was going to happen to output but it may have a very different role now."

Gramlich also said he has worked with Fed board member Alice Rivlin in the past, when both of them worked in the early 1970s at the Brookings Institution. Gramlich served as a senior fellow at the Washington, D.C.-based think tank from 1973 to 1976.

Gramlich said he is proud of his recent work chairing a presidential advisory council on the overhaul of the Social Security System, which recommended that people be allowed to set up individual savings accounts for their benefits.

"I tried to have come out with an approach that a little more built into it with people saving for their own retirement," he said. "You want to have a market instrument that provides complete protection against inflation."
